title: When to Pick the Risky Partner Over the Safe One
documentTitle: Mozilla Board of Directors Slides: Search Partnership Evaluation (Google vs. Yahoo!)
excerptForBlog: Why Google: Users prefer Google; global search performance is the best; dominant brand; familiar experience to users. Mission Alignment: Offer strongest revenue share to date with Google; three-year term; modeling shows all three years over [redacted] mm. Why not Google: Does not promote competition for search; supports the continued dominance of Google; dependency on Google; no revenue guarantee; need product and business focus to succeed; revenue share could drop below projections; no opportunity to grow share; Mozilla must change to focus on search volume/performance; no guarantee. Why Yahoo!: Opportunity to innovate features and services that are customized for Firefox users. Mission Alignment: An agent for change; independence from Google; opportunity to level the playing field in search. Financial Security: High guarantee; 5-year term; diversifies sustainability projects; projected growth of market share. Why not Yahoo!: Search product not currently preferred; low international presence/relevance; users may not be familiar with search experience. Mission Alignment: If unsuccessful, threatens success of both Yahoo! and Mozilla. Financial Stability: Deal may result in business misalignment; limited fallback options. Downside Risks: Contingent on Mozilla's capability to partner deeply; Google may become more aggressive in targeting Mozilla.

lessonTitle: When to Pick the Risky Partner Over the Safe One
pullQuote: Sometimes the best deal isn't the biggest check — it's the one that buys you back your independence.
leadershipTraits: thinks in dependencies, not just revenue
situation: In November 2014, Mozilla's Denelle Dixon-Thayer presented the board with a direct comparison: renew with Google or switch to Yahoo! for search. The stakes were existential — search revenue was Mozilla's financial lifeline, and the document makes clear the choice was between financial comfort and strategic independence.
insight:
The document lays out a clean trap hidden inside the Google option. Google offered better search quality, stronger brand recognition, and — with modeling showing all three years over a redacted revenue figure — seemingly superior economics. But the slide flags something easy to miss: 'no revenue guarantee' and 'revenue share could drop below projections.' The upside was real; so was the downside, and it was uncapped.

Yahoo! flipped the risk profile. The slide credits it with a 'high guarantee' and a five-year term — two features that turn variable revenue into something closer to a fixed floor. The tradeoff is product quality and international reach, both explicitly listed under 'Why not Yahoo!' The hidden strategic move here is classic **switching cost logic in reverse**: Mozilla was evaluating which partner it was more dangerous to stay dependent on, not just which paid more. The note that 'Google may become more aggressive in targeting Mozilla' if Mozilla chose Yahoo! shows the board was thinking about competitive retaliation, not just contract terms.
application: When you're evaluating two partners or vendors, build two columns: expected value and downside floor. A guaranteed smaller number often protects the business better than a projected larger one with no floor. Ask explicitly: if this deal underperforms, what's my fallback? If the answer is 'none,' that's the real risk, not the headline terms.
